author: Adam Carey
title: 'They saved Broad Street': Floyd County thanks first responders to historic courthouse fire - NewsBreak
text:
By Adam Carey ,
9 hours ago Rome-Floyd firefighters receive a standing ovation at the Floyd County Commission meeting Tuesday for their professionalism and skill in containing the blaze that destroyed the historic courthouse. By Adam Carey photos Floyd County officials heaped praise on the Rome-Floyd Fire Department and other first responders for their performance during the devastating fire that destroyed the historic county courthouse.
The Monday fire, which remains under investigation, could easily have spread to the Broad Street downtown district, according to County Manager Jamie McCord.
“We have the best fire department in the state, and maybe even the whole country,” McCord said. “And we will get through this.”
Strong winds from the west fanned the flames, and blew embers and debris onto roofs of several Broad Street buildings. These embers could easily have started new fires, according to McCord, and the leadership of the RFFD quickly recognized that Rome’s downtown was at significant risk.
“The leadership of the fire department needs to be commended on what you guys did,” County Commissioner Scotty Hancock said during the board’s Tuesday meeting. “It’s our leadership that makes us strong, because they have been there a long time and they have seen a lot of situations. They are like a family, brothers to each other.”
Celanese resident Ron Swinford addressed the commission, stating that the fire could have caused untold damage to Broad Street if not for the actions of the fire department.
“They saved Broad Street,” he said.
Fire Chief Troy Brock addressed the crowd, and thanked both the Rome City and Floyd County commissions for their support.
“We had all we needed to fight that fire; we needed nothing else,” Brock said. “We are blessed as a fire department, and we work our tails off to the best of our ability so we can service this community.”
McCord and Brock also singled out County Facilities Manager Ryan Davis and Facilities Supervisor Blake Oyler, who were the first to spread the alarm throughout the historic courthouse and began the evacuation.
Oyler is also credited with turning off the main gas valve, which, Brock said, helped prevent a significant escalation of the fire. Soon after the valve was shut, debris from the roof crushed it, which would have made it impossible to turn off.
“Ryan and Blake gave firefighters at least a 10 minute head start, and probably saved lives by evacuating the building,” McCord said. “This fire could have led to a tremendous loss of life. They should be commended.”
Also during the meeting, commissioners approved a $100,000 emergency allocation to relocate the property tax and vehicle tag offices from the burned out courthouse to the Law Enforcement Center across the street.
McCord explained that county personnel are working to get both operations functional as soon as possible, but that the tag office might not be fully functional until next week because the tag printer machines were destroyed by fire.
He also encouraged anyone who had business with the property tax office recently to check back with the office to confirm paperwork or other transactions have been officially recorded. The phone system should be working as of Thursday morning.
“Although we’re 100% digital at the tax and tag offices, there is a chance that a piece of paper was sitting on a desk waiting to be digitally filed when the fire occurred and could have been lost,” McCord. “Just call the property tax office and confirm that your information and transaction was actually recorded.”
